NOAA's Seafood Import Monitoring Program covers imports of 13 species groups: abalone, Atlantic cod, blue crab (Atlantic), dolphinfish (mahi mahi), grouper, king crab (red), Pacific cod, red snapper, sea cucumber, sharks, shrimp, swordfish and tuna.

Atlantic salmon.historyTitle: Atlantic Salmon — not covered by NOAA's Seafood Import Monitoring Program

lines.text: Salmon is not one of the 13 species groups covered by NOAA's Seafood Import Monitoring Program.
Under USDA country-of-origin labeling rules (7 CFR Part 60), a covered retailer must show the fish's country of origin and whether it is wild-caught or farm-raised.

Country-of-origin labeling rules apply to larger grocery retailers (those licensed under the Perishable Agricultural Commodities Act) and exempt fish markets, butcher shops, and food-service establishments. A processed or value-added item (breaded, marinated, crab cakes) is not covered by these rules at all.

dolphinfish.historyTitle: Mahi Mahi — covered by NOAA's Seafood Import Monitoring Program

lines.text: Covered by NOAA's Seafood Import Monitoring Program.
Imports of this species group must report harvest records to NOAA, including the vessel, catch area and fishing gear. The program does not apply to domestic seafood.
NOAA has denied U.S. market access to some mahi mahi fisheries because of marine-mammal bycatch (as of October 2026):
Ecuador — gillnets
Indonesia — gillnets
Vietnam — gillnets or longlines
Products sold in the U.S. must come from fisheries that were not denied; a counter placard doesn't name the fishery.
Under USDA country-of-origin labeling rules (7 CFR Part 60), a covered retailer must show the fish's country of origin and whether it is wild-caught or farm-raised.

Country-of-origin labeling rules apply to larger grocery retailers (those licensed under the Perishable Agricultural Commodities Act) and exempt fish markets, butcher shops, and food-service establishments. A processed or value-added item (breaded, marinated, crab cakes) is not covered by these rules at all.
